Question six. Why does weight initialization matter? Xavier versus He. That explosion was the starting scale alone. Xavier sets the variance to two over inputs plus outputs, for tanh and sigmoid; He, two over inputs, since ReLU zeroes half of what it sees. And never start the weights equal. Sixteen hidden units started at point oh one end a thousand steps as exact copies, one unit in effect, scoring thirty-eight percent on held-out digits. From Xavier's random start, ninety-eight. Equal units get equal gradients, so nothing ever breaks the tie. Normalization keeps that scale steady in training.

Question seven. What is batch normalization, and how does layer norm differ? Batch norm shifts and scales each feature to mean zero and variance one across the mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift. So the answer depends on the neighbors. This pixel, at half brightness, normalizes to minus two point four beside seven brighter digits, and to plus two point six beside seven darker ones. In a batch of one, a feature is its own mean, so it normalizes to zero whatever the input; hence running averages at inference. Left in training mode and served one request at a time, that layer ignores its input. Layer norm normalizes across one example's features instead: this pixel gets the same value in any batch, or alone. Free of batch size, it's what transformers use. Then, how each step moves.
